50.title: The well of eighty-four steps
50.hook: at Goindval, Guru Amar Das builds a step-well open to every caste
50.tomorrow: first the row, then the audience
50.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit the Baoli Sahib at Goindval, where many walk down the eighty-four steps reciting the Japji and bathing; the well is remembered as a place Guru Amar Das opened to people of every caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water carrier, mocked as homeless on a dark road. Your line was faithful in small things. Whose small, faithful job did you thank? Day fifty.

Imagine being thirsty, standing next to a well full of clean water, and not being allowed to drink from it. Not because it's private property. Because of the family you were born into. For centuries across South Asia, caste decided things like that. Who could draw water from which well. Who could eat with whom. Who could touch whose cup. The man who had carried water for twelve years in the dark was now the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. He settled at Goindval, on the banks of the river Beas. And there he began to dig. Not a normal well. Something grander, and open to everyone. Today, the well.
screen: `THIRSTY, NEXT TO A FULL WELL.` → `CASTE DECIDED WHO COULD DRINK.` → `GURU AMAR DAS BEGINS TO DIG.`

segments.voice: It's called a baoli: a step-well. Instead of lowering a bucket on a rope, you walk down a long staircase into the earth until you reach the water. Step-wells are found across South Asia, some of them wonderfully beautiful. The one at Goindval has eighty-four steps, and it's still there today. Here's what made it different. Guru Amar Das made it open to everyone. Every caste, every family, walked down the same steps and drew from the same water. In a world where a shared well could be a scandal, that was a quiet revolution, built out of brick and stone. It also turned Goindval into a center for the Sikhs, a place people traveled to, and the first great Sikh place of pilgrimage. Now the number. Eighty-four is a significant number in Indian thought. Tradition spoke of eighty-four lakh, or eight point four million, forms of life that a soul might pass through. Sikh tradition says that a person who recites Guru Nanak's Japji on each of the eighty-four steps, bathing at each, can be freed from that long round of births. Many pilgrims still do it, going down step by step. Sikhs hold that practice in different ways: some as a promise, some as a devotional discipline, some as a picture of the long way down to the water of life. But everyone agrees on the first lesson of the baoli. The water at the bottom doesn't know anyone's caste. It's the same for all who walk down to it.
screen: `BAOLI — A WELL YOU WALK DOWN INTO.` · `EIGHTY-FOUR STEPS AT GOINDVAL.` · `OPEN TO EVERY CASTE.` · `A JAPJI ON EACH STEP.` · then, large: `WATER FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink a glass of water slowly. Pour it now if you can. Hold it and look at it. Take one sip, and let it sit in your mouth before you swallow. Then another. Think about where it came from: a river, a reservoir, rain. Think of someone, somewhere, who is thirsty right now. If you pray, you can give thanks for water. Finish the glass slowly. The bell holds the time.
Baoli. A step-well; the one at Goindval has eighty-four steps, and Guru Amar Das opened it to every caste. Today's word.
Your line: water for all. Today, share something basic, water, a seat, a charger, with someone you'd usually pass by. Day fifty.

51.title: First the row, then the audience
51.hook: anyone who comes to see the Guru eats first in langar; tradition says the emperor Akbar sat on the floor too
51.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, langar is served to anyone who comes, seated together in rows on the floor, in pangat; the saying pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat is often quoted to explain why.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baoli, eighty-four steps down to shared water. Your line was water for all. What basic thing did you share with someone you'd usually pass by? Day fifty-one.

Meeting an important person usually works the same way. There's a waiting room. There's a line, and a list, and someone at a desk deciding who goes first. The more important the visitor, the shorter the wait. At Goindval, visiting Guru Amar Das worked differently. Before anyone, anyone at all, could sit with the Guru, they first had to sit on the floor in the langar, the community kitchen, in a row with everyone else, and eat. Farmers, merchants, beggars, priests. And one day, tradition says, the Mughal emperor himself came to Goindval: Akbar. Today, where the emperor sat.
screen: `WAITING ROOMS AND GUEST LISTS.` → `AT GOINDVAL, EVERYONE EATS FIRST.` → `THEN THE EMPEROR ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Sikhs sum up the rule in a short Punjabi saying: pehlan pangat, pichhon sangat. First the row, then the gathering. The pangat is the row of people sitting side by side on the floor to eat. The sangat is the gathering around the Guru. And the order matters. You don't get to the Guru until you've eaten as an equal with everyone else. Tradition says Akbar honored the rule. The emperor sat down on the floor in the row, among ordinary people, and ate the simple food of the kitchen before he met Guru Amar Das. Some tellings add that he was so moved he offered the Guru a grant of land, and the Guru declined it, saying the kitchen should be supported by the community's own work and giving, not by a king. Historians note that the visit comes to us through Sikh tradition, and the details vary. But the rule itself is still kept today. Yesterday it was water. Today it's food. A shared meal says who counts as your equal, and in that world rules of rank and caste said who could sit and eat with whom. The pangat wipes that line out, on the floor, every day. Nobody sits at the head. Nobody gets a higher seat. The same food, from the same pot, served by volunteers. Guru Nanak had begun the langar, and Mata Khivi had kept it going. Guru Amar Das made it the doorway. Before you meet the Guru, you meet your neighbor, at eye level, on the floor.
screen: `PEHLAN PANGAT, PICHHON SANGAT.` · `PANGAT — THE ROW ON THE FLOOR.` · `THE EMPEROR SAT IN THE ROW.` · `NOBODY AT THE HEAD.` · then, large: `FIRST THE ROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat once with no one at the head. Settle, and plan it. Your next meal, or dinner tonight. Sit where you usually don't. Let someone else serve first, or serve everyone yourself and sit down last. If you eat alone, eat on the floor, or at a counter, somewhere without a head of the table. For now, picture the row: faces side by side, all at the same height. The bell holds the time.
First the row. Pehlan pangat: at Goindval, everyone, even an emperor, ate in the row on the floor before meeting the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: first the row. Today, before you meet anyone important, spend a minute with someone nobody thinks is important. Day fifty-one.

52.title: The preachers, women and men
52.hook: he sends out preachers to lead sangats, women among them, and speaks against the burning of widows
52.howItsDone: In Sikh practice any person, woman or man, may lead prayer, read from the Guru Granth Sahib or perform kirtan; Sikhs cite Guru Nanak's words on women and Guru Amar Das's teaching on sati as part of the Gurus' stand for women's equality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, first the row: the emperor on the floor at Goindval. Your line was first the row. Who did you spend a minute with before the important meeting? Day fifty-two.

When something starts to grow, a small business, a club, a movement, there comes a moment when the founder can't be everywhere. People are joining in towns far away. They want to learn, and they can't all travel to one village by the river. That's where the Sikhs were by the time of Guru Amar Das. Communities had sprung up across the Punjab and beyond. So the Guru did something practical. He chose trusted people and sent them out, each to look after a region, teach the hymns and gather the community. And tradition says some of those he trusted with this were women. Today, the seat they sat on.
screen: `THE FOUNDER CAN'T BE EVERYWHERE.` → `COMMUNITIES ACROSS THE PUNJAB.` → `TRUSTED TEACHERS, SENT OUT.`

segments.voice: The word is manji. A manji is a simple cot, a low wooden frame strung with rope, the kind of bed people sat on in Punjabi courtyards. The teacher would sit on the manji, and the community would gather on the ground around it. So manji came to mean the teaching post itself: the seat, and the responsibility that went with it. Sikh tradition speaks of twenty-two manjis set up by Guru Amar Das, spreading the teaching across a wide region. And tradition says women were among those trusted to teach and lead. The Guru also spoke directly about women's lives. One practice of that time and place was sati, the burning of a widow on her husband's funeral fire. In a hymn in the scripture, Guru Amar Das redefines the word. A true sati, he says, is not a woman who burns herself on her husband's pyre; it's one who lives with goodness and contentment, and honors her beloved by how she lives. He is also remembered for discouraging the veil for women at the gathering, and for standing against the idea that a woman's worth ended with her husband's life. Behind all of it is a line of Guru Nanak's that Sikhs quote often. Why call her lesser, he asks, from whom kings are born? We are born of woman, we are married to woman, it is through woman that the world goes on. It's worth being honest: Sikh communities, like others, have lived up to this unevenly. But the Gurus' words are clear, and they're in the book.
screen: `MANJI — A COT, THEN A TEACHING SEAT.` · `TWENTY-TWO MANJIS, TRADITION SAYS.` · `A TRUE SATI LIVES, IN GOODNESS.` · `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · then, large: `SHE IS NOT LESSER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one woman who taught you. Settle, and breathe. It might be a mother or grandmother, a teacher, a boss, an older sister, a neighbor, a friend. Someone who sat, in a way, on a manji for you. Bring her face to mind. Remember one thing she taught you, in words or without them. If she's alive, plan how you'll tell her. If she's gone, just thank her, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Manji. A simple rope cot, and the teaching seat Guru Amar Das gave trusted women and men to lead communities. Today's word.
Your line: she is not lesser. Today, in one meeting or conversation, make sure a woman's voice is heard and credited. Day fifty-two.

53.title: The song of bliss
53.hook: tradition links his great hymn, the Anand Sahib, to joy at a grandson's birth; it is sung at every ceremony
53.howItsDone: The Anand Sahib is part of the Sikh daily prayers, and its first five stanzas with the fortieth are sung at the close of congregational worship and at weddings, namings and funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manji, a rope cot that became a teaching seat. Your line was she is not lesser. Whose voice did you make sure was heard? Day fifty-three.

Good news has a way of tumbling out before the hello is over. Mom, guess what. Guru Amar Das was an old man by now. Tradition says that a grandson was born to his son, Mohri, and the family was full of joy. The baby was named Anand. And around that time, tradition says, the Guru composed a hymn Sikhs still sing at every turn of life. It opens, in effect, with that same rush of good news, told to a mother. Today, the song.
screen: `GOOD NEWS, TUMBLING OUT.` → `MOM, GUESS WHAT.` → `A GRANDSON, AND A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Anand Sahib, the song of bliss. Anand means bliss, deep joy, the kind that settles in rather than flashing past. The hymn has forty stanzas, in raga Ramkali, and its very first line goes something like this, in paraphrase: I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found my true Guru. Notice who the singer turns to with the news: mother, the one who has known the singer longest. And what's the news? Not wealth, not success. The singer has found the true Guru, and with that, the mind is at peace. The hymn goes on to say that this bliss can't be bought or faked, that it comes through the Guru's word, and it sings of the Word ringing inside like music. Tradition links the hymn to the grandson's birth, and the child and the hymn share a name. Here's why you may have heard it without knowing. The Anand Sahib, or its opening stanzas and last stanza, is sung at Sikh ceremonies of every kind. At a wedding. At a baby's naming. At the end of the congregation's prayers. Even at a funeral. Joy, on this path, isn't only for happy days; it's the steady bliss of being close to the Guru, which holds even when life is sad. Those same stanzas are part of Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer. A song that began with a family's joy now closes Sikh gatherings.
screen: `ANAND — DEEP, SETTLED JOY.` · `I AM IN BLISS, O MY MOTHER.` · `THE NEWS: I'VE FOUND THE TRUE GURU.` · `SUNG AT WEDDINGS, NAMINGS, FUNERALS.` · then, large: `BLISS, MOTHER, BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or hum something joyful. Nobody's listening, and it doesn't have to be good. Pick a tune that makes you glad: a lullaby, a hymn from your childhood, a song from a wedding you loved. Hum it softly, or sing it under your breath. Let your chest buzz with it. If a feeling of gladness comes, let it stay a moment. If it doesn't, that's fine; just keep the tune going. The bell holds the time.
Anand. Bliss, deep joy; the name of Guru Amar Das's grandson, and of the hymn that closes Sikh ceremonies. Today's word.
Your line: bliss, mother, bliss. Today, call or message someone who's known you a long time, and share one piece of good news. Day fifty-three.

54.title: Jetha the orphan
54.hook: an orphaned boy selling boiled grams at Lahore comes to Goindval, serves, and marries Bibi Bhani
54.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Ram Das, born Jetha, as the fourth Guru, and tell his orphaned childhood and years of service as a sign that the Gurus chose by devotion, not birth; Bibi Bhani is honored as a pillar of the early community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand, the song of bliss told first to a mother. Your line was bliss, mother, bliss. Who did you share good news with? Day fifty-four.

A crowded market street in Lahore. Carts, dust, shouting. And a small boy with a tray, calling out to passersby: boiled grams, hot boiled grams. Chickpeas, cooked and salted, a street snack that costs next to nothing. His name is Jetha. His parents have both died. He's about seven years old, tradition says, and he's selling snacks on the street to help keep himself alive. This Guru's story begins with almost nothing at all. Today, the boy with the tray.
screen: `A MARKET STREET IN LAHORE.` → `HOT BOILED GRAMS.` → `A BOY NAMED JETHA, ORPHANED.`

segments.voice: Jetha went to live with his grandmother in a village called Basarke, which happened to be the very village Guru Amar Das came from. So when a group of pilgrims set out from there for Goindval, to see the Guru, the young man went with them. And he stayed. He did what Amar Das had once done for Guru Angad: he served. Tradition says he worked on the building of the step-well, carrying baskets of earth, and in the kitchen, and wherever a pair of hands was needed. He didn't come with money or family connections. He came with his work. And someone noticed. The Guru's wife was looking for a husband for their daughter, Bibi Bhani. Tradition says she saw Jetha working and said: a young man like that. The Guru agreed. So the orphan who once sold grams on the street married the Guru's daughter. And Bibi Bhani is honored in her own right. She's remembered for her devoted service to her father, and she would become the wife of one Guru, the mother of another, and the grandmother of a third. Jetha kept serving, for years. Eventually, Guru Amar Das chose him as his successor, and he became the fourth Guru, Guru Ram Das. Notice the baskets. Jetha carried earth for the step-well that was open to every caste, and the boy with nothing became family to the Guru. Sikhs tell it to say that nobody's beginning is too small. The Gurus looked at who people could become, not where they started.
screen: `FROM BASARKE TO GOINDVAL.` · `HE SERVED WITH HIS HANDS.` · `HE MARRIED BIBI BHANI.` · `THE ORPHAN BECAME GURU RAM DAS.` · then, large: `SMALL BEGINNINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer a snack to someone. Settle, and choose who. A coworker, a kid, someone at the bus stop, a person on the street. A handful of nuts, a piece of fruit, a granola bar. Picture Jetha with his tray, and picture yourself holding out yours. Small and simple. For now, just see their face, and plan the moment. The bell holds the time.
Jetha the orphan. The boy who sold boiled grams in Lahore, served at Goindval, married Bibi Bhani, and became Guru Ram Das. Today's word.
Your line: small beginnings. Today, notice someone starting from very little, and give them one word of encouragement. Day fifty-four.

55.title: The pool of nectar
55.hook: Guru Ram Das begins the pool and the town that will be named Amritsar, the pool of nectar
55.howItsDone: Amritsar is the spiritual center of the Sikh world; pilgrims bathe in the sacred pool and walk around it, and many volunteer in its seva, cleaning the tank and serving in the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jetha the orphan, from a tray of boiled grams to the fourth Guru. Your line was small beginnings. Who did you encourage? Day fifty-five.

Most towns grow up around something. A crossroads. A harbor. A mine, a market, a railway station. Take away the thing in the middle and the town doesn't make sense anymore. Today we visit the beginning of one of the most famous cities in the world for Sikhs, a city millions visit every year. And it didn't grow up around a market or a fort. Before it was a city, it was a patch of land with a small natural pond, surrounded by trees. Guru Amar Das, tradition says, asked Jetha, now his son-in-law, to find a place for a new center. And Guru Ram Das began to dig. Today, the pool, and the town that grew around it.
screen: `EVERY TOWN GROWS AROUND SOMETHING.` → `A SMALL POND, AND TREES.` → `GURU RAM DAS BEGINS TO DIG.`

segments.voice: The city is Amritsar. Amrit means nectar, the water of immortality, and sar means pool. So Amritsar is the pool of nectar. In the beginning, the settlement was called Guru ka Chak, the Guru's village, and later Ramdaspur, after Guru Ram Das. The name Amritsar came from the pool itself. Tradition says Guru Ram Das had the pond dug out and widened into a great tank, a sacred pool, and the Sikhs came to help, carrying earth in baskets on their heads, the same work Jetha had once done at the step-well. Here's the practical genius of it. The Guru didn't only build a place of worship. He invited people to come and live there: traders and craftsmen of many kinds, tradition says, so the town would have its own markets and its own living. Worship and work, side by side. It's Kartarpur again, on a bigger scale. There's a story Sikhs tell about the pool too. A young woman named Rajni, married off by her angry father to a man with leprosy, is said to have left her husband by the water while she went for food. He saw a crow dip into the pool and come out white, bathed himself, and was healed. It's a story people tell, and the tree by that spot is still honored. Guru Ram Das didn't live to see the pool finished; that would fall to his son. But he gave it its center. Amritsar grew the way all towns do, around the thing in the middle. It's just that the thing in the middle was a pool of still water.
screen: `AMRIT, NECTAR. SAR, POOL.` · `SIKHS CARRIED EARTH IN BASKETS.` · `TRADERS INVITED: WORSHIP AND WORK.` · `A STORY OF HEALING AT THE WATER.` · then, large: `A TOWN AROUND A POOL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at still water for a minute. A glass of water on the table. A bowl. A puddle, a fountain, a sink you've filled. Settle, and look. Watch the surface go still. Notice the light on it, your reflection maybe, the tiny tremble when you breathe near it. Let your mind settle the way the water does. The bell holds the time.
Amritsar. The pool of nectar; the sacred tank Guru Ram Das began, and the city that grew around it. Today's word.
Your line: a town around a pool. Today, ask what sits in the middle of your days, and whether it's what you'd choose. Day fifty-five.

56.title: The four rounds
56.hook: he writes the four lavan, the wedding hymns that Sikh couples still walk around the Granth to (Suhi, ang 773)
56.howItsDone: In the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, the couple walks four times clockwise around the Guru Granth Sahib as each of Guru Ram Das's four lavan is read and then sung, joined by a scarf.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amritsar, the pool of nectar. Your line was a town around a pool. What sits in the middle of your days? Day fifty-six, the end of a week.

If you've ever been to a Sikh wedding, you've seen it. Morning, in the gurdwara. The couple sits before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture, resting on its raised seat. The bride holds one end of a long scarf, the groom the other. Then the musicians begin to sing, and the couple stands and walks slowly around the scripture, clockwise, the groom a step ahead, the scarf between them. They sit. The singing starts again. They walk again. Four times in all. Every one of those rounds is a hymn, and all four were written by the orphan from Lahore, Guru Ram Das. Today, the four rounds.
screen: `A MORNING WEDDING IN THE GURDWARA.` → `A SCARF BETWEEN THEM.` → `FOUR WALKS AROUND THE SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: They're called the lavan, the rounds. The hymn is in the scripture, in raga Suhi, and it has four stanzas. Each stanza is one round, and each describes a stage, in paraphrase. The first round is about the duties of a good life: following the Guru's teaching, living honestly, remembering God's name. The second is about meeting the true Guru; fear falls away, and the mind is humbled. In the third, the heart fills with longing and love, detached from the world's pull. In the fourth, the mind is at peace, and the soul and God are united as one. Sikhs hear the lavan as two marriages at once. On the surface, a husband and wife, walking into a shared life. Underneath, the soul's marriage to God, the union the hymn keeps singing toward. So the couple isn't only promising themselves to each other. Together, they're walking the soul's path, round by round, with the scripture at the center. The Sikh wedding is called the Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. Remember Anand? And it's usually closed with the Anand Sahib. And look back over the week. The baoli, water for all. First the row, even for an emperor. The manji, and she is not lesser. Anand, the song of bliss. Jetha, the orphan. Amritsar, the pool. And now four rounds, one life. Two Gurus, and one idea running through them: everyone at the same level, walking the same path, with the Word in the middle.
screen: `LAVAN — FOUR ROUNDS, FOUR STANZAS.` · `DUTY, THE GURU, LOVE, UNION.` · `TWO MARRIAGES AT ONCE.` · `THE ANAND KARAJ, CEREMONY OF BLISS.` · then, large: `FOUR ROUNDS, ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a promise you keep. Settle, and breathe. Not one you've broken; one you keep. To a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Maybe you've never said it out loud. Think about when you made it, and every time since that you've kept it, round after round. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If not, just let yourself feel how long you've carried it. The bell holds the time.
Lavan. The four rounds of the Sikh wedding: four stanzas by Guru Ram Das, sung as the couple walks around the scripture. Today's word.
Your line: four rounds, one life. Today, keep one small promise to someone you love, on purpose, and notice it. Day fifty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: walking in circles at a wedding.
what it means: four stages of the soul's path, walked together by a couple, with the scripture at the center.
what a scholar hears: Suhi Chhant of Guru Ram Das, Ang 773–774; each stanza ends by naming its own round, and the fourth opens with the mind in sahaj, settled peace.
